assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — nth Roots
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.instructions: nth roots. Every answer is entered in a step-by-step tool: write the radicand as a perfect power, take the root, and decide whether absolute value bars are needed — the tool checks each step. You have 3 tries on each Warm-Up, Classwork and Practice question, with hints. The Exit Ticket is one try with no hints.
assignment.teacherNotes: Algebra II Honors, Radicals Lesson 1 (nth Roots), from the district slides, TEKS A2.7G. Warm-Up rebuilt as readiness: powers → perfect powers → √(x²) = |x|. Every Classwork item is a slide example with its Check Your Progress; "Simplify" answers are graded by value AND form (simplest radical form, bars only where needed). CW3, the numerical radicals √63 and 3√12, comes before the variable examples so students find the largest perfect-square factor with numbers first; the other items keep the slides’ order. Two audited Digital SAT items from the CCMR bank sit in Practice, and the Honors extension items (P12, P13, P11) are DOK 3–4, so the Honors version is ready as written. Warm-Up and Exit Ticket are generated per student and back Recovery. Slide note: the "Simplify" slide gives √(9x⁴y¹⁰z⁴) = 3x²y⁵z²; with y allowed to be negative it is 3x²|y⁵|z², which CW10 teaches. Slide note: CW9’s Check Your Progress is ∛(8(x + 2)¹⁵) = 2(x + 2)⁵, because the slide’s ∛(27(x + 2)⁹) is 3(x + 2)³, the example’s own answer, which a student could copy.

steps.title: Why it matters today
steps.instruction: A square root undoes a square and a cube root undoes a cube. Writing the radicand as a perfect power is how you take the root.

questions.prompt: Square roots and absolute value. Evaluate $\sqrt{ {{s}} }$, $\sqrt{(-{{r}})^2}$ and $\sqrt{({{t}})^2}$. Then decide what $\sqrt{x^2}$ equals for every real number $x$.
directionSteps: Evaluate each square root.
Decide what the square root of x squared equals for every real number.
hints: What number is under each radical once you work out the inside? Can it be negative?
The radical sign √ means the principal (nonnegative) square root.
Which rule gives a nonnegative answer for every x, including a negative x?

misconceptions.message: √ means the principal square root, which is never negative.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √ always gives a value that is…

steps.title: Principal square root
steps.instruction: The radical sign √ means the nonnegative square root: √25 = 5, never −5.

steps.title: Absolute value
steps.instruction: Squaring hides a sign, so √(x²) gives back the size of x: √(x²) = |x|.

solutionReview.headline: Squaring loses the sign, and √ is never negative.
reasoning: (−{{r}})² = {{r2}} and √{{r2}} = {{r}}: the answer is positive even though the base was negative.
So √(x²) = |x| for every real x: x when x ≥ 0 and −x when x < 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing √((−{{r}})²) = −{{r}}: a principal square root is never negative.

questions.prompt: New vocabulary. In $\sqrt[5]{32}$, the small 5 is the index and 32 is the radicand. A number $a$ is an $n$th root of $b$ when $a^n = b$. Name the parts of $\sqrt[5]{32}$, and then find both real fourth roots of 81.
directionSteps: Name the index.
Name the radicand.
Choose the statement that proves the root.
Find both real fourth roots of 81.

responses.label: Which statement shows that 2 is a fifth root of 32?
The other real fourth root of 81

hints: Which number is written small in the radical sign, and which is under it?
Which number, used as a factor 4 times, gives 81? Its opposite works too.
The principal root is the nonnegative one.

misconceptions.message: The principal root is the one that is not negative.

steps.title: nth root
steps.instruction: For real numbers a and b and a positive integer n, if aⁿ = b, then a is an nth root of b.

steps.title: Radical sign, index, radicand
steps.instruction: In ⁿ√b the symbol √ is the radical sign, n is the index and b is the radicand. √b means index 2.

steps.title: Principal root
steps.instruction: When b has two real nth roots, the nonnegative one is the principal root, written ⁿ√b. ±ⁿ√b names both.

solutionReview.headline: Read the parts, then undo the power.
reasoning: The index is 5 and the radicand is 32; 2⁵ = 32, so 2 is a fifth root of 32.
3⁴ = 81 and (−3)⁴ = 81. The principal fourth root is 3; the other is −3.
solutionReview.answerSummary: index 5, radicand 32; fourth roots of 81: 3 and −3
solutionReview.commonError: Calling −3 the principal root: the principal root is the nonnegative one.

questions.prompt: Real nth roots. Sort each set of roots by how many REAL roots it has. Use the index (even or odd) and the sign of the radicand. Then give a reason for each group.
directionSteps: Look at the index: even or odd.
Look at the sign of the radicand.
Sort each card into a group.
Give a reason for each group.
hints: For each card: is the index even or odd, and is the radicand positive, negative or 0?
An odd index always gives exactly one real root. An even index gives two when the radicand is positive.
No real number raised to an even power is negative. And 0 has only one root: 0.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A real number raised to an even power is never…

steps.title: Even index
steps.instruction: a > 0: two real roots, ±ⁿ√a. a < 0: no real roots. a = 0: one root, 0.

steps.title: Odd index
steps.instruction: a > 0: one positive root. a < 0: one negative root. a = 0: one root, 0.

solutionReview.headline: Even or odd index, then the sign of the radicand.
reasoning: Even index, positive radicand: two real roots (±7, ±2, ±2).
Odd index: exactly one real root (−4 and 2); and 0 has only the root 0.
Even index, negative radicand: no real root, because an even power is never negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Putting the cube roots of −64 under "No real roots": an odd index takes a negative radicand to a negative root, −4.

questions.prompt: Example B, then Check Your Progress B. Simplify $-\sqrt{(q^3+5)^4}$. Decide whether absolute value bars are needed. Then simplify $-\sqrt{(a^3+2)^8}$.
directionSteps: Write the radicand as a perfect square.
Take the principal square root and keep the negative sign in front.
Decide whether absolute value bars are needed.

responses.label: Why are absolute value bars not needed?
options: (q³ + 5)² is never negative, so it is already the principal root
responses.answer: (q³ + 5)² is never negative, so it is already the principal root

hints: Treat q³ + 5 as one block. What power of that block, squared, gives (q³ + 5)⁴?
The negative sign is outside the radical. Take the principal root first, then make it the opposite.
(q³ + 5)⁴ = [(q³ + 5)²]². A square is never negative, so no bars are needed.

misconceptions.message: The negative sign in front of the radical stays in your answer.
The negative sign in front of the radical stays in your answer.

steps.title: A binomial base
steps.instruction: Treat (q³ + 5) as one quantity: (q³ + 5)⁴ = [(q³ + 5)²]².

steps.title: The opposite of a principal root
steps.instruction: −√b is the opposite of the principal square root of b.

solutionReview.headline: One block, a perfect square, then the opposite.
reasoning: The opposite of the principal root is −(q³ + 5)².
In the same way, (a³ + 2)⁸ = [(a³ + 2)⁴]² and (a³ + 2)⁴ is never negative, so −√((a³ + 2)⁸) = −(a³ + 2)⁴.
solutionReview.commonError: Dropping the negative sign, or halving the 3 inside the base: only the outside exponent is halved.

questions.prompt: Example D, then Check Your Progress D. Decide whether $\sqrt{-4}$ is a real number, and name its two imaginary square roots. Then simplify $\sqrt{-16}$.
directionSteps: Decide whether the first root is a real number.
Name its two imaginary square roots.

responses.label: √(−4) is…
options: not a real number: the index is even and the radicand is negative
responses.answer: not a real number: the index is even and the radicand is negative

responses.label: The two imaginary square roots of −4 are

i is the imaginary unit, and i² = −1. Which multiple of i squares to −4?
Both 4i and −4i square to −16.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A real number raised to an even power is…

steps.title: Even index, negative radicand
steps.instruction: There is no real root. In the complex numbers there are roots: i = √(−1), so √(−4) = 2i, and −2i is the other square root.

solutionReview.headline: No real root; two imaginary roots.
reasoning: The index is even and −4 < 0, so √(−4) is not a real number.
(2i)² = 4i² = −4 and (−2i)² = −4, so the square roots are 2i and −2i.
Similarly, the square roots of −16 are ±4i.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing (−2)² = −4: the square of a negative number is positive.

questions.prompt: Simplify using absolute value (even index). Simplify $\sqrt[6]{t^6}$ and $\sqrt[4]{x^4}$, then $\sqrt[4]{16x^4y^8}$. Here $t$, $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. Explain when absolute value bars are needed.

options: x may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative; y² is never negative
Every variable outside an even root needs bars
y² needs bars too, because y may be negative
responses.answer: x may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative; y² is never negative

hints: If t = −2, what is t⁶, and what is its sixth root? Is that t, or something else?
What monomial, to the fourth power, gives 16x⁴y⁸? Which of its factors can be negative?
16x⁴y⁸ = (2xy²)⁴. Bars go only around a factor that can be negative: x can, y² cannot.

misconceptions.message: Your answer is right when t ≥ 0. Try t = −1.
Your answer is right when x ≥ 0. Try x = −1.
Your answer is right when x ≥ 0. Try x = −1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For an even index n, ⁿ√(aⁿ) equals…

steps.title: Even index
steps.instruction: ⁿ√(aⁿ) = |a| when n is even, because the principal root is nonnegative and a might not be.

steps.title: Only where needed
steps.instruction: x², y⁴ and every even power are already nonnegative, so they need no bars.

solutionReview.headline: Even index: bars around anything that can be negative.
reasoning: y² is never negative, so it needs no bars.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 2xy²: if x = −1 and y = 1, the root is 2 but 2xy² is −2.

questions.prompt: Simplify using absolute value (odd index). Simplify $\sqrt[5]{243(x+2)^{15}}$ by writing the radicand as a fifth power. Then simplify $\sqrt[3]{8(x+2)^{15}}$.
directionSteps: Write the radicand as a fifth power.
Decide whether absolute value bars are needed.
Simplify the second expression the same way.

responses.label: 243(x + 2)¹⁵ = [ ? ]⁵. This base is the fifth root.
Does ⁵√(243(x + 2)¹⁵) need absolute value bars?
options: No — the index is odd, so the root keeps the sign of 3(x + 2)³
Yes — every binomial root needs bars
No — because x + 2 is always positive
responses.answer: No — the index is odd, so the root keeps the sign of 3(x + 2)³

hints: Which number to the fifth power is 243? Which power of (x + 2), to the fifth, gives (x + 2)¹⁵?
Treat x + 2 as one block and divide its exponent by the index. Is the index odd or even?
243 = 3⁵ and (x + 2)¹⁵ = [(x + 2)³]⁵. An odd root keeps the sign, so no bars. For the cube root, divide 15 by 3.

misconceptions.message: An odd root keeps the sign, so it needs no absolute value bars.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For an odd index n, ⁿ√(aⁿ) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Write the fifth power; odd roots keep the sign.
reasoning: The index is odd, so ⁵√(243(x + 2)¹⁵) = 3(x + 2)³, with no bars.
8(x + 2)¹⁵ = [2(x + 2)⁵]³, and the index is odd again, so ∛(8(x + 2)¹⁵) = 2(x + 2)⁵.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding absolute value bars to an odd root: |3(x + 2)³| is wrong when x < −2.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{9x^4y^{10}z^4}$, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ can be any real numbers. Write the radicand as a perfect square first. Use absolute value bars only where they are needed.
directionSteps: Write the radicand as a perfect square.
Take the principal square root.
Decide which factor needs absolute value bars.

responses.label: Why does only y⁵ need bars?
options: y⁵ is negative when y is negative; x² and z² never are
x² and z² are always positive, and y⁵ is always negative
responses.answer: y⁵ is negative when y is negative; x² and z² never are

hints: Which number squared is 9? What power of each letter, squared, gives x⁴, y¹⁰ and z⁴?
The square root of a square is the absolute value of its base. Which factors of that base can be negative?
9x⁴y¹⁰z⁴ = (3x²y⁵z²)². Of 3x², y⁵ and z², only y⁵ can be negative.

misconceptions.message: Your answer is right when y ≥ 0. Try y = −1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √(y¹⁰) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Halve the exponents; bars only where a factor can be negative.
reasoning: √((3x²y⁵z²)²) = |3x²y⁵z²| = 3x²|y⁵|z², because 3x² and z² are never negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 3x²y⁵z² (as on the slide): when y = −1 that value is negative, but a square root is never negative.

questions.prompt: Multiply radicals. Simplify $2\sqrt{8a^2}\cdot 4\sqrt{18a^2}$. Multiply the coefficients, multiply the radicands, then take the square root.

√m · √n = √(mn), and a² is never negative, so √(a⁴) = a² with no bars.

misconceptions.message: The Product Property multiplies the radicands; it does not add them.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √m · √n equals…

solutionReview.headline: Coefficients times coefficients, radicands times radicands.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the radicands (8a² + 18a²) instead of multiplying them.
